reviews.title: AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models
reviews.author: Chip Huyen
reviews.review: Very informative read. Somewhat receptive and unfortunately a wee bit dated (which I suppose is inevitable with this topic) but glad I got through it and took rigorous notes.

reviews.title: The Bonfire of the Vanities
reviews.author: Tom Wolfe
reviews.review: Unbelievable. Genuinely one of the best books I’ve read. It feels a bit like *Succession*, except written so many years earlier — almost every character is unbelievably unlikeable, but they’re written so brilliantly that you can’t stop reading. Watching everything unravel and seeing each of them get their comeuppance is incredibly satisfying. It’s genuinely hard to put down. I really, really loved it.

reviews.title: The Psychology of Money: Timeless Lessons on Wealth, Greed, and Happiness
reviews.author: Morgan Housel
reviews.review: Extremely interesting and compact book. I don't think it necessarily told me anything too surprising but it is interesting. I like the Daniel Kahneman quotes and examples to get into my dumb dumb brain very practical advice on finance without it ever being condescending. But don't expect a guide on getting rich. Its main take away is: invest and leave it for as long as possible.

reviews.title: Twilight of the Habsburgs: The Life and Times of Emperor Francis Joseph
reviews.author: Alan Warwick Palmer
reviews.review: Not going to lie, book was a bit of a slog, but Francis Joseph is an interesting character. Very sympathetic and deeply tragic. Desperately trying to stop a war and usually doing the right thing, only to be surrounded by people determined to make the worst possible decisions.

reviews.title: The Killer Angels (The Civil War Trilogy, #2)
reviews.author: Michael Shaara
reviews.review: Really great Gettysburg account that does the impossible and puts Lee in a sort of bad light. Forgotten heroes and great action. A bit overly whimsical on men's eyes and ground. But beautifully written and great emotional heft.

reviews.title: Between Two Fires
reviews.author: Christopher Buehlman
reviews.review: Reads like Dark Souls the book meets Last of Us. Very good. Lost the plot towards the end. I began thinking at the beginning of this book about why it has not been turned it into a TV series and at the end totally got why. Regardless, great horror, based in the 1300s that I've been recommending to a bunch of folks and really glad I picked up.

reviews.title: Fox 8
reviews.author: George Saunders
reviews.review: It feels a bit off putting this in my read pile given it's 75 pages and large font but here we are. Great emotional guy wrenching Pixar film of a book. Loved every few pages of it.

reviews.title: Principles of Product Management: How to Land a PM Job and Launch Your Product Career
reviews.author: Peter Yang
reviews.review: For quite a short book it does repeat itself a bit but I appreciate the PM interviews and all the practical advice. I feel like it would have benefited from diving into the different types of PM (analytical, machine learning and data platform) rather than remaining surface level but I did like that it was so surface-level that I could read about these things to pique my interest further. Overall, I think this is a great introduction but as with most tech adjacent content I pickup wish it went a little more in-depth.

reviews.title: The Need to Be Whole: Patriotism and the History of Prejudice
reviews.author: Wendell Berry
reviews.review: This is a great book that I partially ruined for myself by listening to it as an audiobook. I've learned that some books work brilliantly in audio form and others don't, and this is firmly in the latter category. Wendell Berry is unquestionably a thoughtful writer and a passionate advocate for agriculture. His reflections on the damage caused by neglect, short-term thinking, and a lack of investment in rural communities are compelling. Some of his views feel dated or debatable, but there's no denying the sincerity or beauty of his writing. In many ways, he comes across as a remarkably progressive thinker for someone writing from the perspective of American farmland.

reviews.title: Killed to Order: China's Organ Harvesting Industry and the True Nature of America's Biggest Adversary
reviews.author: Jan Jekielek
reviews.review: It's a far from perfect's book but I think it's very important. It's very one-sided. The author doesn't shy away from the fact that he is falun gong and he does go on a few tangents but I think you are entitled to an unbalanced argument when it comes to the topic of organ harvesting. The evidence while thin is strong and I didn't really want to read this book but glad I did. The story of Maggie at the beginning and appendix part one at end is very good.

reviews.title: Zen on the Trail: Hiking as Pilgrimage
reviews.author: Christopher Ives
reviews.review: Wow. Whata book. Exactly what Zen and The art of Motorcycle should have been. Sometimes a bit of a listicle but really amazing insight into Japanese zen though the very practical lens of hiking. Very inspiring for a rando library book.

reviews.title: Small Things Like These
reviews.author: Claire Keegan
reviews.review: Really enjoyed this. It delivers a poignant and deeply moving story with the absolute mastery of less is more. I think this one will really stick with me for bringing to light something very sinister and real.

reviews.title: Great Classic Science Fiction
reviews.author: H.G. Wells
reviews.review: The quality was not good at first. Particularly H G Welles then it sort of got better. I liked Philp K Dick and the guy who wrote Hyperion where good. Much of it is forgettable and I struggled to get it finished. Which in glad I did as the best stuff was at the end.

reviews.title: Confessions of Anthony Fauci
reviews.author: Robert Kennedy III
reviews.review: Absolutely God awful ai slop. Too lazy to even get rid of the classic m-dash of AI. Every page is "that's not x. That's y. And that means z' which is such lazy AI writing. I knew what I was getting into with this read and was saving an ironic 5* rating but there's so much disinformation in this book that it makes me want to take a shower and I still feel gross having read it. Also he uses the word firewall every 3rd page and never correctly. Funny joke. Terrible terrible book.

reviews.title: The Civil War (American Heritage)
reviews.author: Bruce Catton
reviews.review: Loved it. Terrible present for Katy but fantastic for moi. So much simpler and cooler than the British Civil War. It makes me want to learn more. I wish the images were better and that it felt a bit more personable, but it’s an excellent account of what happened and a great complement to Ken Burns’s series.

reviews.title: The Blazing World: A New History of Revolutionary England, 1603-1689
reviews.author: Jonathan Healey
reviews.review: The Bishops' Wars period is pretty confusing. It often feels like no one really knows what they want, and the key figures aren’t exactly consistent either. There’s this strong anti-Catholic sentiment, but at the same time you’ve got a king in Charles I who’s tied up with it Later Cromwell people back him for a while, then later they literally dig him up and put his head on display. The book doesn’t help with this. It throws a lot of people at you without sticking to a clear narrative, so it’s easy to lose track of what’s going on. That said, once you fill in some of the gaps yourself, it does start to make sense. I ended up having to look a few things up, but after that the sequence of events and the different wars fit together somewhat.

reviews.title: Albert Camus's The Stranger
reviews.author: Harold Bloom
reviews.review: It’s like reading a dream. It’s really good. You can really feel the hot, sticky heat and how absurd it is that people attach abstract ideas to life. It’s a very effective piece of writing.

reviews.title: The Things They Carried
reviews.author: Tim O'Brien
reviews.review: Very raw and honest book. Particularly emotional towards the end where Tim recounts all the people in the war and in his life he lost. Really excellent book. I didn’t appreciate as much repeated narratives over and over - which I get reflects the rumination out in the bush but it was a bit overdone. Regardless the accounts were very poignant and the book served as a great companion to the the fantastic Ken Burns documentary which finishes with Tim reading the opening of this book.

reviews.title: The Quiet American
reviews.author: Graham Greene
reviews.review: I was going to give the only 5* as a joke to RFK Jr’s weird ai piece but this book deserves it. Such a great snapshot of the French controlled era and an utter joy to read on my travels through Vietnam. On top of that I loved the romantic and murder plot. A beautifully flawed narrator who ties the whole thing together with both a great wit and journalistic style. Not my favorite book of all time but deserves my first 5*.

reviews.title: Among the Thugs
reviews.author: Bill Buford
reviews.review: this started like a 5-star book but ran out of steam. too much naval-gazing about the nature of crowds. but when he's describing the action he's like Bill Bryson at his best.

reviews.title: A Prayer for the Crown-Shy (Monk & Robot, #2)
reviews.author: Becky Chambers
reviews.review: It’s very twee, but I do enjoy some solarpunk. I wish it were a little more grounded and philosophical, but it’s an enjoyable romp. I think I enjoyed the first one a bit more.

reviews.title: Where the Deer and the Antelope Play: The Pastoral Observations of One Ignorant American Who Loves to Walk Outside
reviews.author: Nick Offerman
reviews.review: He describes national parks very well, and I’m very excited to read Wendell Berry and Aldo Leopold. I really liked his bit with his mates, including Jeff from Wilco. It came off very Bill Bryson, very funny. But then he gets a bit too haughty, like a celebrity on a high horse, and tells us how America is broken and how it should work. He’s not wrong; I just think it comes off a bit disingenuous.

reviews.title: Erasure
reviews.author: Percival Everett
reviews.review: I really wanted this to be better. I loved the concert, and I love the writing because it was very intelligent and perceptive. It's a shame, because the concept was amazing. It's definitely not as good as James.

reviews.title: Permafrost
reviews.author: Alastair Reynolds
reviews.review: Very cool time-travel thriller. Extremely compact. So much is explored in such a short period of time. I did think the anti-AI elements could have been a bit more fleshed out, and some of the story beats were a bit silly. But it’s really terrific sci-fi, and I highly recommend it.

reviews.title: The Sun Also Rises
reviews.author: Ernest Hemingway
reviews.review: Interesting. It reads like Seinfeld set in Europe. It took me a second to get into it, and I thought the Paris sections were dreadfully dull, but I really liked the prose and the descriptions of all the bullfighting. Unfortunately, it also reveals Hemingway as a massive anti-Semite, so I think this is probably where he and I part ways.

reviews.title: Let's Explore Diabetes with Owls: Essays, Etc.
reviews.author: David Sedaris
reviews.review: Twee observations that are sort of funny. I got this book purely for the title as a gift for someone else. I would give it one star, but I agree with his opinions on China, garbage collection, and journaling. So two stars it is, David.

reviews.title: Don’t Tell the President: The Best, Worst, and Mostly Untold Stories from Presidential Advance ― A Funny Insider Account
reviews.author: Jean Becker
reviews.review: A series of short stories about the adventures of advance agents. It started off not very well, but I really got into it. I especially liked the story about the agents who, thinking it was a Russian bug, took apart a chandelier that crashed onto the floor below. Enjoyable, if somewhat superfluous, reading.

reviews.title: Voice for the Voiceless: Over Seven Decades of Struggle with China for My Land and My People – A New York Times Bestselling Memoir of Spiritual Exile and Freedom
reviews.author: Dalai Lama XIV
reviews.review: You can really feel the struggle this poor guy has gone through, being exiled his entire life and unable to return to Tibet. Despite that, he just wants to cooperate peacefully rather than seek full independence from the Chinese government. It’s a bit verbose, but the underlying message is very touching, and it reads like it’s a terrible situation over there. A very illuminating read.

reviews.title: James
reviews.author: Percival Everett
reviews.review: Questionable narrative choices, but what a brilliant book. Heartbreaking, funny, and such a great play on the original Huckleberry Finn, and better in almost every way except for the ending. I really enjoyed it. I can’t wait to see the future Spielberg film, but oy it has some pretty bleak moments in it.

reviews.title: Buddha Volume 2: The Four Encounters
reviews.author: Osamu Tezuka
reviews.review: Brilliant, unsettling, and deeply imaginative, the work captures one of the most consequential moments in the Buddha’s life: his rejection of the kingdom. Tezuka's style is erratic jumping between the ancient world to modern anachronisms, fourth wall breaks and absurd humor (fat jokes!) to incredible graphic violence and explicit language. But the whiplash feels masterful and adds to the absurdity. Even the art style is in extremes, pages dissolve into scrawled doodles and then into lavish splash pages of dense jungle landscapes. Tezuka is often titled as the originator or "father" of manga and in true absurd and chaotic style he weaves a great tale. Can't wait for volume three.
